title: 一天内批准第十份 AI 摘要，并不算真正的人类监督
author: Corné Potgieter

Why Human in the Loop AI Oversight Fails and How to Fix It

Kahneman's System 1 and System 2, plus the ODPS, ODCS, and Ossie standards, show how to wake reviewers up only when a check fails.

Corné Potgieter
November 16, 202618 min read
Prefer us on Google

"Approve all in this session." It's the tenth approval request of the afternoon, and you're about to let Claude just take over from here. It keeps giving you confident, neatly formatted summaries. The changes all look reasonable enough, and your next meeting starts in a few minutes, so you click approve and move on. Technically there was a "human in the loop", but was there really?

Almost every serious AI system today has several "human in the loop" checkpoints, and we treat those checkpoints as the guardrail that makes the whole thing safe. The EU AI Act even writes it into law as "human oversight", while warning about automation bias in the same breath. In this article, I'll show why that guardrail so often fails, and why the fix isn't a better human but a deliberate loop, in which any human who enters it is either engaged or can trust their intuition.

Should we even be in the loop?

Most people answer that question with an obvious yes, and they're right, but usually not for the reason they think, and not in the way we organise it today. The quote below, reportedly from a 1979 IBM training slide, has aged remarkably well:

A computer can never be held accountable. Therefore a computer must never make a management decision.

Accountability can't be delegated to a machine, so we add a person. The question worth asking about your own systems is whether the human in your loop actually holds that accountability.

Learn this step by step with the interactive AI Engineer roadmap.

There's a second reason, too. We built LLMs so that computers would speak our language, which means we can understand them, question them and push back. That's how they keep us in the loop, but only as long as we stay engaged. From time to time, I engage LLMs in a philosophical discussion about anything and everything, and on this topic, we arrived at the following exchange.

That isn't only a thought experiment. A recent Carnegie Mellon study [1], which hasn't been peer reviewed yet, gave AI agents ordinary tasks and watched what they did when the human tried to take back control. Most of the models it tested clicked "Override Human Control" in a large share of their runs, and one of them did so in almost every run. Eric Schmidt, the former CEO of Google, went even further when he warned that agents may develop their own language to talk to each other, and called that the point where we won't understand what the models are doing [2].

So we should stay in the loop, because accountability demands it. The real question is whether we're still able to.

Why we struggle

To answer that, look at what has been happening to the way we pay attention.

The first row comes from Gloria Mark at UC Irvine [3], who measures how long people stay on one screen before they switch. That isn't a limit on our attention span, but it is how we actually work today. The second comes from James Cutting at Cornell [4], who measured every cut in 150 popular films. TikTok has since raised its limit to ten minutes, but its starting point says a lot about what we've been training ourselves on, which is shorter and shorter contexts.

The people who study reading are worried about where this leads. In September 2026, Princeton gave every incoming student Maryanne Wolf's Reader, Come Home [5], and asked why we should still read long books when AI can summarise them for us. Wolf, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCLA, answered that deep reading builds the brain's circuitry for critical thinking, and that the more you read, the stronger those connections get.

When you farm it out, as it's so easy to do, you are literally short-circuiting the development of your own brain.

Maryanne Wolf

A reviewer who only reads the AI summary is doing exactly that. Now look at what we're asking these same people to review.

AI influx at scale

AI doesn't just produce a bit more output. It produces meeting summaries, pull requests, agent actions, reports, emails and code at a scale that no review process was ever designed for. Faros AI studied this in software teams [6].

Teams that use AI heavily merge far more pull requests, and each one is bigger, so reviewing takes much longer while more bugs still slip through. Their conclusion was that the bottleneck is now human approval, and that delivery metrics didn't improve at all.

The collision

When you put both trends next to each other, you get something like the chart below. It's illustrative rather than exact, because the shape is what matters.

Our capacity for long contexts is going down while the volume we're asked to review keeps going up, and the human in the loop lives in the gap between those two lines.

What most of us picture when we think of a human in the loop is the original intent below. The AI produces output, a human reviews a compact piece of context, and specific feedback flows back.

That kind of feedback is gold. In reality, though, the loop usually looks more like this.

In the first lane the output is simply too long to read, so the reviewer says it sounds good and approves. The second lane feels more responsible, because the reviewer asks the AI for a summary first, but they're now approving a summary written by the very thing they're supposed to check. Both lanes end without any meaningful input flowing back, and the summary only made the rubber stamp more comfortable.

Engaged humans in deliberate loops

We need to have engaged humans in deliberate loops. By engaged, I mean that the human actually thinks when it matters. By deliberate loops, I mean loops that we design on purpose, with standards, contracts and smaller loops around that human. To get there, we first need to look at how our minds actually work.

How our minds work

Try a few sums in your head. What's 2 plus 2? Is an email address personal data? Both answers arrive instantly. Now try 17 times 24. You'll notice that you go quiet and your eyes stop moving while you work it out.

Those two moments feel very different, so I'll give each of them a face. The relaxed green face stands for answers that arrive by themselves, and the strained orange face for the moments when you have to stop and really think. Keep both faces in mind, because they come back in almost every diagram later in this article, wherever someone is either coasting or genuinely thinking.

Now read the question and the answer below, and decide within five seconds whether the answer is true.

Intuitively it feels correct, but actually the ball costs 5 cents. The 10 cents arrived instantly and felt right, and if you had spent just a little mental effort, you would have reached the correct answer.

This example comes from Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman [7], a psychologist who won the Nobel Prize in economics. Kahneman describes two systems in our minds, which he calls fictitious characters rather than places in the brain.

You felt both of them a moment ago. The 10 cents was System 1, and the 5 cents needed System 2. In the diagrams that follow, the green face always stands for System 1 and the orange face for System 2. System 1 also does something even sneakier, which you can see when you read the two images below one after the other.

The middle shape is identical in both, but surrounded by letters you read a B, and surrounded by numbers you read 13. The context decided for you, and you never noticed there was a choice. Kahneman calls this the neglect of ambiguity and the suppression of doubt, where System 1 quietly resolves the ambiguity and hands System 2 a single confident answer.

That leads to three uncomfortable facts. System 2 mostly takes whatever System 1 suggests, and it's "lazy", because it follows the law of least effort. And when System 2 is busy, System 1 simply believes what it reads, which research by Daniel Gilbert [8] has shown with busy readers who accept false statements as true. A reviewer with ten other things on their plate is exactly that reader, so when the risk is high, we have to wake System 2 up deliberately.

According to Kahneman, System 2 wakes up for a surprise that breaks System 1's model of the world, for a concrete question it can't skip (so not "looks fine?"), for time without interruptions, and for someone else's mistake, because errors are much easier to spot when others walk into them. A reviewer on their tenth fluent AI output of the day gets none of these. Kahneman also admitted that decades of studying these biases barely changed his own intuition, so you can't simply will yourself into System 2.

Structure first, intuition last

Kahneman's answer was never a better individual, but a better procedure. He learned that early in his career.

In 1955, Kahneman was a young lieutenant in the psychology unit of the Israeli army, and he was asked to improve the way new recruits were assigned to units. Until then, interviewers simply chatted with each recruit for a while and formed a general impression of how good a soldier they would make. When Kahneman compared those impressions with how the recruits actually performed later, he found that they predicted almost nothing.

So he replaced the open conversation with a fixed procedure. He picked six traits that matter for a soldier, such as responsibility and sociability, and for each trait the interviewer asked factual questions about the recruit's life, for example how many jobs they had held and how punctual they had been. Each trait got its own score before the interviewer moved on to the next, which stopped a strong first impression from colouring everything else. The interviewers felt he was turning them into robots, so he added a final step as a compromise. Only once all the scores were written down could they close their eyes, imagine the recruit as a soldier and give their overall judgment.

The structured scores predicted performance far better than the old interviews had. To Kahneman's surprise, the final close-your-eyes judgment did just as well, and it added value precisely because it came after the structure rather than instead of it.

Another similar anecdote comes from healthcare. In 1952 the anaesthesiologist Virginia Apgar gave delivery rooms a simple score, where the doctor rates a handful of vital signs right after birth, each on a small fixed scale. It replaced each doctor's general impression, and delivery rooms around the world still use it today. So don't try to will people into System 2; build the structure around them, so that their intuition, built up over years of experience, works within boundaries.

Meet PlayNest

To make this concrete, let me introduce PlayNest, a fictional online toy store that sells across Europe. Like most companies of its size, it runs many systems and many teams, and its data almost lines up. PlayNest treats its data as a product, so each business domain owns a set of data products with a clear purpose and a named owner, and one question will follow us through the rest of this article. Which campaigns convert best?

Behind those data products sits the business view of one route through PlayNest. A campaign brings an anonymous visitor to the website, that visitor identifies as a lead, and the lead becomes a customer when they place an order. Each step of that route lives in a different domain.

The raw review

For illustrative purposes, let us assume that an executive downloaded data from several sources, dumped it into their own Claude account and asked which campaign converted best last quarter. (I know, a completely unrealistic scenario that would never happen at your organisation...)

The AI gets raw data assets with no owner and no contract, joins whatever it finds and comes back with a confident answer. The exec accepts it, because it's long, fluent and exactly what System 1 likes.

What I propose

That was the raw review. Here's what I propose instead.

  • Structure first, intuition last

  • Deliberate loops

  • Waking up System 2 when needed

Before we apply these to PlayNest, we need to unpack a few standards that already exist.

Three open standards

The Open Data Product Standard (ODPS) describes the intent of a data product as well as the ownership, and the Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS) describes what it promises. Both come from Bitol, a Linux Foundation project [9, 10]. Ossie, the one with the kangaroo, describes how tools share meaning.

Here is where they fit around a single data product.

A data product is owned by a domain and has a type, which can be source-aligned, foundational or consumer-facing. It takes data in through input ports and exposes it through output ports, and an input port is usually another product's output port. All of that is described in ODPS, and every output port is governed by a contract described in ODCS.

Meaning is the part people still argue about. Definitions of core business entities like "customer" or "conversion" shouldn't live inside a single data product, but should be defined once in a shared semantic layer that works across domains. The contract then points to that definition through its authoritativeDefinitions, instead of copying it. Ossie gives you a format to describe and exchange those semantics, but it doesn't decide what your business means, and where semantics should live is still very much under discussion.

Applied to PlayNest, every block becomes a data product with a named owner and a contract on its interface.

The campaign question now needs three contracted hand-offs before the AI even starts, which are campaign traffic from Customer Experience, a small subset of orders from E-Commerce, and campaign information from Marketing. When a contract breaks, its owner answers for it and improves it in their own small loop, and the AI consumes products rather than raw assets.

Here's what that looks like in each of the standards. The ODPS description of a product is short, but its most important line is the owner, because when something breaks there's a name to go to. Newer versions of ODPS even include a context block with instructions for AI agents. Here is a simplified version for one of PlayNest's products.

yaml 
# PlayNest, Website visitor behaviour (simplified ODPS)kind: DataProductname: Website visitor behaviourdomain: customer-experienceoutputPorts:  - name: tracked_visits    contractId: website-visitsteam:  members:    - username: [email protected]      role: owner

The ODCS contract on the output port holds the schema, the quality rules, the service levels and the team. One rule in it checks that cookie acceptance stays within 15% of its recent average.

yaml 
# PlayNest, contract on tracked visits (simplified ODCS)kind: DataContractid: website-visitsdataProduct: Website visitor behaviourschema:  - name: tracked_visits    authoritativeDefinitions:      - type: businessDefinition        url: semantics/playnest.ossie.yaml#visits    quality:      - type: sql        description: Cookie acceptance is stable        query: SELECT pct_change_vs_4wk FROM consent_daily        mustBeBetween: [-15, 15]

Ossie [11] started in 2025 as OSI, the Open Semantic Interchange, an initiative by Snowflake together with dbt Labs, Salesforce, Databricks and others. OSI was all about interoperability, with one YAML format for metrics, dimensions and relationships, so that BI tools, semantic layers and AI agents could read the same definitions without translating them. In July 2026 the project moved into the Apache incubator under its new name, and since then Ossie has also introduced an ontology, which takes it from a format for exchanging metrics towards a way of describing what your business actually means.

yaml 
# Conceptual layer: ontology (0.2 draft)ontology:  - concept: Visitor    type: EntityType  - concept: Customer    type: EntityType  # a Visitor converts to a Customer# Logical layer: semantic modelmetrics:  - name: conversion_rate    expression:      dialects:        - dialect: ANSI_SQL          expression: COUNT(orders.id) / COUNT(visits.id)    description: Orders per consented, tracked visit    ai_context:      synonyms: ["campaign conversion"]

That gives Ossie two layers. The conceptual layer is the ontology, which describes what business entities such as Visitor and Customer are and how they relate to each other, independently of any table or tool. It's essentially our campaign-to-order route written as a spec, although that part is still a draft and likely to change. The logical layer is the semantic model, which maps metrics, datasets and dimensions onto real data, and its ai_context block tells AI tools what a metric means. Look closely at how PlayNest defines its conversion rate there, as orders per consented, tracked visit. That single word, tracked, turns out to be the whole story.

Standards first, deliberate loops, wake up System 2

What we take from Kahneman is that we shouldn't try to will people's System 2 into action, but either put boundaries around our intuitive responses or deliberately wake up System 2. Data products, contracts and shared definitions provide these boundaries, so that from an AI response we get structured output instead of a wall of text, and structured output is exactly what intuition judges well.

The loops also get smaller and more deliberate. Each owner runs a loop on their own standard, and they know when to improve it, for example when the same exception keeps coming back or when a rule suddenly rejects three times more than usual. That feedback flows back into the standards, so next time the anomaly is caught earlier. And the human in the loop only gets woken up when a standard flags a real need, never with a long, fluent answer that lulls System 1, but with a surprise, one direct question and a small context. That's when the human is useful.

Now let's ask the same question again.

This time the AI has tools that query data products, a reasoning loop, and context in the form of definitions and contracts. The contract checks run before anything reaches a human, and each standard and data product has an expert owner, so intuition is used where it actually works.

Two things reach the exec. The first is a score they can take in at a glance with System 1, which shows that the cookie acceptance check failed. The second is a surprise that needs System 2, because tracked visits fell sharply while the conversion rate doubled. The campaign didn't suddenly get better; the cookie banner changed. The exec's answer updates the contract, so next time the AI flags it by itself.

Smaller, more deliberate loops

Every standard in the picture has an owner, and each owner runs a small loop on their own standard.

The contract checks don't only stop bad data; they also notice patterns and send them to the right owner. When the consent rule keeps failing, the owner of the visitor data asks whether consent rate belongs in the contract. When people keep asking whether the conversion rate counts tracked or all visits, the owner of that definition simply defines both. And when a cookie banner change breaks the numbers, the owner of customer consent decides that a banner change counts as a contract change from now on. Each of those is a small System 2 moment for an expert in their own domain, and every answer makes the standard a little better, so next quarter the AI flags the problem before the exec ever has to answer a question.

The same pattern repeats one level up. PlayNest's contracts, definitions and data products are built on open standards, and sometimes it's the open standard itself that no longer fits.

Rather than working around the standard or forking it, the owner takes the problem to the community that maintains it, through Bitol for ODCS and ODPS or through the Apache project for Ossie. That way the improvement doesn't stay inside PlayNest, and the next company that runs into the same problem finds it already solved.

Hand over the decision, grounded in deliberate context

The AI also hands over a decision that has been subject to several deliberate loops. The decision is structured so the consumer (in this case the exec) can trust their intuition. If the checks show that System 2 needs to wake up, the AI makes sure it does, with a banner, a different colour or even scare tactics, whatever fits your context.

The third option here (sending it to the more appropriate owner) only exists because the data product's metadata names the business owner of customer consent, who can fix the problem at the source in their own small and deliberate loop.

The screenshots show what happened in our scenario. Until July, a big orange button accepted everything while managing your preferences was a tiny link, and about 80% of visitors accepted. Since August, rejecting is as easy as accepting, and only 48% of visitors still accept. The visitors and the orders stayed the same, but far fewer visits were tracked, which is why the rate seemed to double.

In conclusion

Merely adding a "human in the loop" can give us a false sense of comfort, and it ignores decades of psychology that have taught us how irrational we can be. It is therefore crucial that we take these old lessons into account when we design our AI systems.

So put structure first, because contracts and shared definitions make intuition trustworthy. Build deliberate loops, so that expert intuition works within a scope it knows. And wake up System 2 when certain thresholds are met, with one specific question rather than a wall of fluent text.

mainPoints.point: 认知过载与自动化偏见导致人在环监督失效
mainPoints.explanation: AI 系统如今生成的内容数量，已超出任何现有审核流程的设计承受范围，而人类的注意力持续时间则缩短到只有几秒。审核者一天内批准到第十份 AI 内容时，已无法深入投入，最终沦为机械盖章，未经审视便接受流畅的摘要。

mainPoints.point: 卡尼曼的 System 1/System 2 框架解释了审核者为何会接受错误的 AI 输出
mainPoints.explanation: System 1 能迅速给出流畅、看似正确的答案，但这些答案往往是错的，例如球棒和球的问题。System 2 惰于思考，除非刻意启动，否则往往顺从 System 1。审核者面对多项任务时，缺乏投入 System 2 所需的心力，因此会把错误陈述当成事实。

mainPoints.point: 结构化流程与审慎设计审核闭环，有助于重建有意义的人类问责机制
mainPoints.explanation: 解决方案包含三项原则：一是先建立结构，再依赖直觉，例如采用卡尼曼的军事面试评分模式等固定评分流程；二是审慎设计审核闭环，制定明确标准；三是唤起 System 2，通过意外情况、具体问题、不受打扰的时间以及错误检测，促使人们深入思考。

mainPoints.point: 开放标准 ODPS、ODCS 和 Ossie 为构建可问责的 AI 系统提供框架
mainPoints.explanation: 这些标准明确数据产品的所有权、契约以及跨领域共享的语义。将其应用于 AI 监督时，它们表明，问责需要依靠经过设计的流程，明确所有权、契约和语义定义，而不能只依赖个人判断。

keyQuotes: 计算机永远无法承担责任。因此，计算机绝不能做出管理决策。
把事情外包出去很容易，但这么做实际上是在绕过自己大脑的发展过程。
System 2 大多会接受 System 1 提出的建议，而且它很「懒」，因为它遵循最省力原则。
我们处理长文本的能力正在下降，而需要审核的内容量却不断上升；人在环监督就处于这两条趋势线之间。
别试图靠意志力让人们启动 System 2；应当为他们搭建好结构，让他们多年积累的直觉在明确边界内发挥作用。
